title: The hidden compass that flies pigeons home
topic: How do pigeons find their way home?

lines: Take a pigeon somewhere it has never been, and it still flies home.
Most researchers think its compass is the sun, read with an inner clock.
Shift that clock with artificial light, and on a sunny day the bird loses its bearings.

beats.title: Clock-shifted pigeons
lines: But on cloudy days, those same clock-shifted birds navigate correctly.
That suggests they can use Earth's magnetic field, and magnets strapped to their backs disrupt it.
In one German study, pigeons wearing a small magnet headed off further right than birds carrying brass weights.

beats.title: Where is the sensor?
lines: Where that sense sits is still debated, with suspects in the nose, the inner ear and even the liver.
So next time a pigeon circles after take-off, watch closely: one researcher suggests it's mapping very low sound waves.

sources.claim: Pigeons find their way home from distant places they have never visited; map and compass model; compass appears to rely on the sun; altering perceived time of day with artificial lighting affected homing
Time-shifted pigeons cannot orient on clear sunny days but navigate correctly on overcast days, suggesting magnetic orientation; disrupted by magnets attached to their backs
Magnet pigeons released around a loft in Germany vanished deflected to the right of controls carrying brass weights; magnetic sense located in the nasal region
Location of the pigeon magnetic sense debated: trigeminal system, inner ear (2025 study), superparamagnetic macrophages in the liver
Research by Jon Hagstrum suggests pigeons use low-frequency infrasound and fly in a circle when first taking off to map it
